## Parallel directions {#fv4-parallel .fv-lesson .relation-lesson }

```{=html}
<p>Parallel lines have <strong>parallel direction vectors</strong>.</p>
<div class="relation-direction-layout">
  <div data-parallel-directions></div>
  <div>
    <div class="fv-equation"><span data-math="\color{#217864}{\underset{\sim}{d_2}}=k\color{#315985}{\underset{\sim}{d_1}},\qquad k\ne0"></span></div>
    <p>The vectors can point in the same or opposite directions.</p>
    <p>The same idea applies in two or three dimensions.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

<div class="booklet-cue">Booklet §3.3 · pp. 51–52</div>

::: {.notes}
Connect to the known criterion for parallel vectors; no component calculation is needed here. The fixed 3D projection shows two distinct parallel lines with their direction arrows in opposite senses. The blue arrow represents d1 and the green arrow represents d2=−2d1. No coordinates are required. Direction vectors must be non-zero. Parallel directions alone do not distinguish distinct parallel lines from coincident lines; the next slide develops that geometric distinction. Ask: “Would reversing an arrow change the direction of the line?” The pale xy-plane and vertical z-axis provide spatial context; there is no camera to manipulate.
:::
